content: Cardamom refers to herbs belonging to two genera within the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, specifically Elettaria and Amomum. These plants produce small seed pods that are triangular in cross-section and spindle-shaped, with a thin, papery outer shell and small black seeds inside. The pods of Elettaria are light green, while those of Amomum are larger and dark brown. Types of Cardamom and Their Distribution The two main genera of the ginger family that are classified as cardamom are distributed as follows: Elettaria (commonly known as green cardamom or true cardamom) is found from India to Malaysia. Amomum (commonly referred to as black cardamom, brown cardamom, Kravan, Java cardamom, Bengal cardamom, Siamese cardamom, white cardamom, or red cardamom) is primarily distributed across Asia and Australia. Uses Cardamom is widely used as a cooking spice and in traditional medicine. Elettaria cardamomum is commonly used as a spice, a masticatory (chewing substance), and in medicinal applications. It is sometimes smoked and serves as a food source for the larvae of the moth Endoclita hosei. Amomum is a key ingredient in traditional medicine systems in China, India, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. In the Middle East and Turkey, green cardamom powder is used to flavor sweet dishes, coffee, and tea. It is also incorporated into some savory recipes. In Arabic, cardamom is called al-Hayl. In South Asia, green cardamom is a common ingredient in traditional Indian sweets and tea (chai). Black cardamom is often used in garam masala spice blends for curries and is referred to as Moti Elaichi (fat cardamom) in Hindi and Urdu. In Malayalam, the language of Kerala (which produces 70% of India’s cardamom), it is called Elakka. In Northern Europe, cardamom is frequently used in sweet foods. Cardamom is also used in the production of gin. Culinary Uses Around the World Cardamom has a strong, unique flavor and an intensely aromatic fragrance. It is a staple in Indian cooking and is often used in baking in Nordic countries. Despite being one of the most expensive spices by weight, only a small amount is needed to impart its distinctive flavor. Cardamom is best stored in its pod form, as the seeds lose their flavor quickly once exposed or ground. However, high-quality ground cardamom is a more affordable and convenient alternative. For recipes requiring whole pods, a common substitution is 10 pods for 1½ teaspoons of ground cardamom. Traditional Medicine In South Asia, green cardamom (known as Elaichi in Hindi and Urdu) is widely used to treat dental and gum infections, throat ailments, lung congestion, pulmonary tuberculosis, eyelid inflammation, and digestive disorders. It is also reportedly used as an antidote for snake and scorpion venom. Species within the genus Amomum are also utilized in traditional Indian medicine. For example, Amomum villosum is used in traditional Chinese medicine to treat stomachaches, constipation, dysentery, and other digestive issues. Tsao-ko cardamom, cultivated in Yunnan, China, is used both medicinally and as a spice.
